abstract: Nodal roots are critical determinants of maize productivity and resilience, but the molecular mechanisms governing their development remain poorly defined. Transcriptome analyses across three stages of maize brace root (aboveground nodal roots) development identified the squamosa promoter binding protein (SBP) transcription factors tasselsheath4 (TSH4), unbranched2 (UB2), and unbranched3 (UB3) as negative regulators of brace root initiation. Analysis of single, double, and triple mutants revealed a dose-dependent increase in the number of nodes with brace roots and a non-linear increase in the number of brace roots per node. The increased number of brace roots within a node resulted from a physical expansion of the stem pulvinus and de-repression of brace root initiation programs, which resulted in two tiers of brace roots at each node. Downstream analyses revealed that SBP TFs negatively regulate liguleless2 expression, which acts in concert with liguleless1 to promote brace root initiation, and phytohormone analysis identified a mechanism whereby sbp mutants exhibited increased ACC accumulation. Differential levels of gibberellin (GA4) were identified between tsh4 and ub2;ub3 mutant nodes. The differential levels of gibberellin regulated primordia expansion resulting in distinct brace root phenotypes - tsh4 mutants had fewer, thicker brace roots whereas ub3 mutants had more and thinner brace roots. The tsh4 and ub3 GA4-mediated post-initiation expansion mechanism was also found to underlie natural variation in brace root size and number. Together, our findings identify SBP transcription factors as central regulators of brace root initiation and primordia expansion and show that altering developmental trajectories can alter brace root architecture.
